citeAs: Mihaylov, T., Clark, P., Khot, T., and Sabharwal, A. (2018). Can a Suit of Armor Conduct Electricity? A New Dataset for Open Book Question Answering. EMNLP 2018.
creator: Todor Mihaylov, Peter Clark, Tushar Khot, Ashish Sabharwal (Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence; Heidelberg University)
description: OpenBookQA is a multiple-choice question answering dataset modeled after open book exams. It consists of about 5957 4-way multiple-choice questions paired with a set of 1326 elementary level science facts (the "open book"). Answering questions requires combining an open book fact with broad common knowledge, probing multi-hop reasoning beyond simple retrieval.
name: OpenBookQA
rai:annotationsPerItem: 5 independent crowd worker annotations per question (for answerability verification)
rai:annotatorDemographics: Workers from North America with a 'masters' level qualification on Amazon Mechanical Turk.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human performance was estimated at approximately 92% on the Test set. A conservative lower bound of H̃(Q) − 3% with probability over 98.8% was derived using Hoeffding's Inequality. Additional validation on 100 randomly chosen questions from each of Train, Dev, and Test sets yielded 88.6%, 90.2%, and 91.6% respectively.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: A crowd worker was shown a random science fact f from the set F, asked to think of a second common fact k that may be combined with f to derive a new valid assertion, then convert it into a 4-way multiple-choice question. The system verified basic checks (4 choices, no negation words, uniform choice length). The worker then fed the question to an IR solver and a word-association solver to verify neither could answer it correctly. The question was then shown to 5 new crowd workers; if at least 4 of 5 answered correctly, it was deemed answerable. Answer choices were randomly shuffled to avoid bias. Dev and Test splits were further filtered by an in-house expert.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset has inevitable human bias from crowdsourcing: a "plausible answer detector" (ignoring the question) achieves 49.6% accuracy, and an "odd-one-out" solver achieves 50.2%, both well above the 25% random baseline. Choice 'A' was the correct answer in 69% of questions before shuffling. Workers generally start with the correct answer and then create three incorrect ones, which tend to be homogeneous or share common properties uncharacteristic of the correct answer.
rai:dataCollection: Questions were generated via a multi-stage crowdsourcing and partial expert filtering process. Crowd workers were shown a science fact from the open book, asked to think of a second common fact, then create a 4-way multiple-choice question. Questions were filtered for hardness (must fool IR and word-association solvers), answerability (at least 4 of 5 crowd workers must answer correctly), and answer choice de-biasing. Dev and Test splits were further filtered by an in-house expert.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The open book F consists of 1326 science facts drawn from a subset of the WorldTree corpus (Jansen et al., 2018), specifically from the 2287 WorldTree facts marked as "central" in at least one explanation, further filtered to those general enough to be applicable to multiple situations.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset has inevitable human bias from crowdsourcing. In 21% of analyzed Train questions, the crowdsourced question tests for a fact that doesn't necessarily need the original science fact. The additional facts K provided by workers were often incomplete, over-complete, or only distantly related to the question. Even with oracle facts, the best model achieves only ~76%, far from human performance of 92%, suggesting non-trivial reasoning challenges remain.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Answer choices were randomly shuffled to avoid unintended positional bias (Choice 'A' was the correct answer in 69% of questions before shuffling).
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The 2287 WorldTree facts marked as "central" were filtered down to 1326 that appear general enough to be applicable to multiple situations. Questions were filtered for: exactly 4 answer choices, no negation words, and uniform answer choice length (all with at most 3 or at least 4 words). Answer choices were randomly shuffled to avoid positional bias.
rai:dataUseCases: Open book question answering; evaluating multi-hop reasoning combining provided science facts with broad common knowledge; benchmarking QA systems on elementary-level science questions; studying knowledge retrieval and reasoning in NLP systems.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: An information retrieval (IR) solver (Clark et al., 2016) and a word association based solver (Turney, 2017) were used during question generation to verify that neither could answer the question correctly, ensuring hardness.

evidence.name: We present a new kind of question answering dataset, OpenBookQA, modeled after open book exams for assessing human understanding of a subject.
evidence.description: We present a new kind of question answering dataset, OpenBookQA, that consists of two parts: Q, a set of 5957 multiple-choice questions, and F, a set of 1326 diverse facts about elementary level science.
evidence.url: The dataset and the code for the models are available at http://data.allenai.org/OpenBookQA .
evidence.creator: Todor Mihaylov and Peter Clark and Tushar Khot and Ashish Sabharwal. Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Seattle, WA, U.S.A. Research Training Group AIPHES & Heidelberg University, Heidelberg, Germany
evidence.publisher: yAllen Institute for Artiﬁcial Intelligence, Seattle, WA, U.S.A.
evidence.inLanguage: We present a new kind of question answering dataset, OpenBookQA, modeled after open book exams for assessing human understanding of a subject. The open book that comes with our questions is a set of 1326 elementary level science facts.
evidence.isLiveDataset: OpenBookQA consists of 5957 questions, with 4957/500/500 in the Train/Dev/Test splits.
evidence.citeAs: Todor Mihaylov and Peter Clark and Tushar Khot and Ashish Sabharwal. Can a Suit of Armor Conduct Electricity? A New Dataset for Open Book Question Answering.
evidence.rai:dataCollection: We used a multi-stage process starting with F, using crowd-sourcing to generate (noisy) questions based on F that probe novel situations, using an automatic filter to ensure hardness for retrieval and association based systems, using a crowd filter to ensure answerability by a lay person, and further using an expert filter to ensure higher quality in Dev and Test sets.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: We used a multi-stage process starting with F, using crowd-sourcing to generate (noisy) questions based on F that probe novel situations, using an automatic filter to ensure hardness for retrieval and association based systems, using a crowd filter to ensure answerability by a lay person, and further using an expert filter to ensure higher quality in Dev and Test sets.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: We used Amazon Mechnical Turk, with workers from North America and with a 'masters' level qualification.
evidence.rai:annotatorDemographics: We used Amazon Mechnical Turk, with workers from North America and with a 'masters' level qualification.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: A crowd-worker w is shown a random science fact f from the set F. w is asked to think of a second common fact, k, that may be combined with f to derive a new, valid assertion s. w then converts s into a question-answer pair and extends this into a 4-way multiple choice question by adding 3 incorrect answer choices.
evidence.rai:annotationsPerItem: Question qmc is then shown to 5 new crowd-workers, who are asked to answer it. If at least 4 out of 5 workers answer qmc correctly, it is deemed answerable and the process continues.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: As an additional assessment, we also obtained 5 new annotations for 100 randomly chosen questions from each of Train, Dev, and Test sets. The performance remained similar at 88.6%, 90.2%, and 91.6%, resp.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: For F, we use a subset of the WorldTree corpus which Jansen et al. (2018) have analyzed for sufficiency for elementary level science. The subset we use is taken from the 2287 WorldTree facts that were marked as "central" by the original authors in at least one explanation. We further filter them down to 1326 that appear general enough to be applicable to multiple situations.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The subset we use is taken from the 2287 WorldTree facts that were marked as "central" by the original authors in at least one explanation. We further filter them down to 1326 that appear general enough to be applicable to multiple situations.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: Motivated by recent findings of gameability of NLP datasets (Gururangan et al., 2018), we also develop and evaluate simple, attention-based, neural baselines including a plausible answer detector (which ignores the question text completely) and an odd-one-out solver. These highlight inevitable human bias in any crowdsourced dataset, increasing performance on OpenBookQA to 48%.
evidence.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The answer choices of qmc are randomly shuffled to avoid unintended bias. Choice 'A' was the correct answer in 69% of the questions at the end of Step 4.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: We leave it as a challenge to solve the retrieval problem in this multi-hop setting and to close the large gap to human performance.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: We leave closing the large gap to human performance as a challenge for the NLP community.
evidence.rai:machineAnnotationTools: w then feeds the multiple-choice question qmc to an information retrieval solver (Clark et al., 2016) and a word association based solver (Turney, 2017), and verifies that (a) neither of them answers qmc correctly and (b) the top 3 IR retrieved sentences are insufficient to answer qmc; if not, the question is edited and re-tried.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: In 21% of the cases, the crowdsourced question actually tests for a fact that doesn't necessarily need the original science fact. These second facts, unfortunately, were often incomplete, over-complete, or only distantly related to q. We thus include in OpenBookQA the set K of such second facts only as auxiliary data for optional use. We emphasize that K should not be viewed as 'gold' additional facts, or as a substitute for broad common knowledge.
